description: Project Nightlock is an interactive platform that uses NASA’s SPHEREx data to explore the infrared universe and investigate potential clues to distant objects such as Planet X.
summary:
NightLock Sky Explorer is a browser tool that lets anyone compare real NASA SPHEREx observations without downloading FITS files or installing astronomy software. For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we processed 1,172 images of five known targets and built five ways to compare them over time: Time-lapse, Blink, Side by Side, Difference, and Stack.

Visitors can choose a target from a sky map, compare observations in the same detector band, or use a chart to explore changes in brightness. In our tests, Barnard’s Star moved at 9.8–10.5 arcseconds per year across six detector bands, close to the published value of 10.39. RW Aurigae shows a different kind of change: it varies in brightness without the clear position shift seen in Barnard’s Star.

NightLock makes archived NASA data easier to explore and teach with. It demonstrates known motion and variability without claiming to discover Planet X.
details:
What we built

NightLock Sky Explorer makes it possible to look at the same patch of sky on different dates and see what changed. A visitor can choose one of five targets from a sky map, search by name or coordinates, and compare observations within the same detector band. The five targets are Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

How it works

We downloaded calibrated SPHEREx Level 2 FITS observations from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive. Each observation can have a different pointing or orientation, so we used its sky-coordinate information to align images onto a shared grid for each target. We grouped observations by detector and applied a consistent display scale within each group. This reduces visual changes caused by switching wavelength bands or rescaling each image separately. We then exported 1,172 lightweight PNG frames and a JSON file containing observation dates, detector information, and other metadata. The browser loads these prepared files. Visitors do not need to download or process the raw FITS files themselves.

What visitors can do

Time-lapse plays observations in date order. Blink alternates between two selected dates so a moving source appears to jump against the background. Side by Side lets visitors inspect both dates together. Difference highlights where one frame is brighter than the other. Stack averages aligned frames so stationary sources can stand out while a moving source may appear stretched. Visitors can also inspect a relative-brightness chart and select a plotted point to open the corresponding observation. The brightness values come from measurements on the calibrated images, not from the display PNGs.

What we tested

We compared motion estimated from the images with published reference values. Barnard’s Star measured 9.8–10.5 arcseconds per year across six detector bands, compared with a published value of 10.39. Epsilon Indi B measured 4.0–5.2 arcseconds per year across five bands, compared with 4.71. WISE 0855−0714 was too faint for reliable tracking in individual frames. That result is important because the viewer should show where the data are inconclusive, not make every apparent shift look like a detection.

Tools, design, and impact

We used Python, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, and Pillow for data processing and export. The Explorer uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas. We adapted the classic blink-comparator technique for the browser and paired it with a sky map and an interactive brightness chart. A teacher can use the same tool to demonstrate how a nearby star moves and how a variable star brightens or fades, without setting up specialist software. The prototype covers five preprocessed targets and archived observations. It is not a live telescope feed, an all-sky search tool, or a claim of a new planet discovery.
